title: Many Readers, One Writer: Why the Mutex Gets Slower and shared_mutex Starves the Writer

questions.question: A pose is read by 8 threads and written by 1. It is behind a mutex. What happens to the total read rate as readers are added, measured?
options: It falls: 8 readers got about a fifth of what one reader did
It rises with the number of readers
questions.explanation: Every read takes the same lock. Measured 40774, 10093 and 8503 reads per millisecond at 1, 4 and 8 readers. A mutex serialises readers and moves its cache line between cores on every acquisition.

questions.question: shared_mutex allows many readers at once. With 8 readers, how many writes did the writer manage, out of about 14,000 wanted?
options: About 14,000, since the writer is unaffected
questions.explanation: Readers kept arriving before the last left, so the writer never got in. It was also slower for readers than the plain mutex it replaced. The standard does not say whether a writer is preferred, so code must not depend on either. Count what the writer completes, not only what the readers do.

questions.question: A reader's data copy overlaps a write. How does a seqlock reader know to throw the copy away?
options: It reads the counter before and after
It compares the value with the last one
questions.explanation: Odd means a write is in progress, and a different value afterwards means one landed, so it retries. Forced on one thread in the suite: a write landed between the data read and the second counter read, the reader retried once, and returned the new value whole.

questions.question: The seqlock copied its data with memcpy produced 0 torn reads in 200000 writes. Why is it still wrong?
options: Reading memory another thread may be writing, without atomics, is a data race in C++ whatever the hardware does, and clang 14's thread sanitizer reported 20 in 5 runs
It is not wrong; it never failed
questions.explanation: GCC 11's sanitizer reported nothing on the same code. A real race that works, which one tool finds and the other misses. The fix is the data held as atomic words with relaxed accesses between the fences.

questions.question: With the writer in a tight loop and no pause, 3 readers got 21,117 reads and 501,504 retries. What does that say about where a seqlock fits?
options: Readers starve against a value rewritten continuously, about 24 retries per read
questions.explanation: It suits a value that changes in bursts, not one rewritten as fast as possible. Spaced writes, 20 microseconds apart, cost a few retries each. The number to watch in production is retries() against reads.

questions.question: A Seqlock<std::string> is refused at compile time. Why?
options: The compiler cannot hash a string
The reader copies raw bytes while a writer may be changing them
questions.explanation: A string's bytes are a pointer to memory the writer could free, so a copy taken mid-write could be dereferenced before it is discarded. The type must be trivially copyable. A static_assert on std::is_trivially_copyable, proved by checks/. A refusal at compile time, where a run-time crash would have been the alternative.
